text: tory forms of juvenile idiopathic arthritis.1,2,4,8 The tu- mour necrosis factor inhibitor etanercept, which is licensed for paediatric use in many countries, produces excellent responses in many patients with polyarthritis, particularly those who are rheumatoid-factor positive.8 Like methotrexate, it may be less effective in those with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.2 Infliximab, al- though unlicensed, also seems to be of benefit,1,2,8 and may be more effective than etanercept in the treatment of associated uveitis.2 Other drugs that have been tried with some evidence of benefit include abatacept, adali- mumab, tocilizumab, and anakinra;1,2,8 there is some evi- dence that the latter, an interleukin-1 receptor antago- nist, may be more effective than the tumour necrosis factor inhibitors in treating patients with systemic arthri- tis.2 • Many other drugs have been tried in juvenile idiopath- ic arthritis, often on the basis of effectiveness in adults. Sulfasalazine may be of benefit in late-onset oligoarthritis1 but adverse effects are often trouble- some.8 Concern about adverse effects may also have limited the use of cytotoxic and immunosuppressant drugs other than methotrexate, and there are few con- trolled studies,8 although benefit has been reported with leflunomide in polyarticular disease.1,8 Thalidomide has been suggested for treatment-resistant systemic arthri- tis.1 In very severe unremitting disease, autologous bone marrow transplantation has been tried.1,7,8 Drug treatment aimed at the complications of disease, rather than the disease process itself, may be needed. There is some evidence that bisphosphonates may be useful in controlling low bone mineral density and fragility frac- tures associated with juvenile idiopathic arthritis.1,9 Growth hormone has also been widely used to moderate the severe growth retardation that is often seen.1 Topical treatment with glucocorticoids and mydriatics may be needed for eye disease.1 Physiotherapy and occupational therapy are also important components of disease management, and surgery may be needed in selected cases.1 1.
